title: Magna Carta
author: King John of England
openingText: JOHN, by the grace of God King of England, Lord of Ireland, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to his archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, barons, justices, foresters, sheriffs, stewards, servants, and to all his officials and loyal subjects, Greeting. KNOW THAT BEFORE GOD, for the health of our soul and those of our ancestors and heirs, to the honour of God, the exaltation of the holy Church, and the better ordering of our kingdom... TO ALL FREE MEN OF OUR KINGDOM we have also granted, for us and our heirs for ever, all the liberties written out below, to have and to keep for them and their heirs, of us and our heirs.
about:
Magna Carta is the charter signed by King John of England at Runnymede in June 1215, under pressure from rebellious barons. Its 63 clauses cover specific medieval concerns — taxation, feudal dues, the use of forests, the fate of foreign mercenaries — and a few principles that have echoed through history: that the king is subject to law, that no free man may be imprisoned or punished without lawful judgment, that justice cannot be sold or refused.

Magna Carta was issued, repudiated, and reissued multiple times in the 13th century. It became foundational over centuries — invoked by 17th-century parliamentarians against the Stuarts, by 18th-century American colonists against George III, and by 20th-century declarations of human rights. The actual document is mostly about feudal land law. The myth it became is one of the foundations of constitutional government.

whyItMatters.title: The King Is Subject to Law
whyItMatters.body: The principle that even a king cannot act outside the law is the most important political idea in Magna Carta. It was not new in 1215, but the Charter put it in writing in a way that could be cited and enforced. Eight hundred years of constitutional government rest on this single claim.

whyItMatters.title: Due Process Begins
whyItMatters.body: Clause 39 — that no free man may be seized, imprisoned, dispossessed, or destroyed except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land — is the foundation of due process in every common-law system. The American Fifth Amendment is its descendant.

whyItMatters.title: A Document That Outgrew Itself
whyItMatters.body: Most of the 63 clauses concern medieval matters that have nothing to do with modern law. But the few principles that did matter were powerful enough to make the whole document the symbol of constitutional government. The myth is larger than the text. Both are worth knowing.

angleCards.title: The political crisis behind the charter.
angleCards.text: Who were the rebel barons, and what had John actually done? The charter emerged from a specific breakdown — lost wars, extortionate taxation, the king's habit of taking hostages, selling offices, and overriding feudal custom whenever it suited him. Reading with this angle means tracking which clauses address which abuse, and understanding Runnymede as a transaction, not a revolution.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Magna Carta as a response to a specific political crisis — understanding what King John had actually done to provoke the barons, what specific remedies each clause was designed to provide, and why the settlement collapsed within months.

angleCards.title: The Clause 39 lineage.
angleCards.text: One clause — no free man seized or imprisoned except by lawful judgement of his peers — became the cornerstone of eight centuries of constitutional law. Reading with this angle means tracing a single idea: how forty words written for medieval barons became habeas corpus, the Fifth Amendment, and the legal bedrock of liberal democracy.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the lineage of Clause 39 through the document itself and then forward through history — understanding what it meant in 1215, how its meaning expanded, and how it became the foundation of modern due process.

angleCards.title: The medieval feudal world.
angleCards.text: The Magna Carta is dense with terms that have no modern equivalent: scutage, relief, wardship, seisin, mort d'ancestor. Reading with this angle means decoding that vocabulary and seeing the document as a picture of a working feudal society — how land was held, inherited, and taxed, and what obligations flowed between lords, vassals, and the king.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Magna Carta as a window into medieval feudal society — using each clause as a source of evidence about how land tenure, inheritance, debt, and royal justice actually worked in 13th-century England.

angleCards.title: Constitutional origins.
angleCards.text: The Magna Carta is often called the first constitutional document. But what does that mean? The 1215 version was annulled, reissued, revised, and reinterpreted across centuries before it became a symbol. Reading with this angle means asking how a failed peace treaty between a king and his barons came to underpin American democracy, international human rights law, and the modern concept of the rule of law.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Magna Carta as the origin point of constitutional government — asking how its specific feudal provisions became universal principles, and what that transformation tells us about the relationship between legal texts and the societies that interpret them.

cast.name: King John
cast.description: King of England from 1199 to 1216. John was an intelligent but erratic ruler who had lost Normandy to France in 1204, then spent a decade levying ever-heavier taxes to fund campaigns to reclaim it. His abuse of feudal custom — extortionate reliefs, arbitrary seizures, hostage-taking, the sale of royal offices — united the barons against him. He signed the charter intending to repudiate it at the first opportunity, and he did.

cast.name: Stephen Langton
cast.description: Archbishop of Canterbury and the key broker at Runnymede. Langton had been at the centre of the dispute between John and Pope Innocent III for years, and he used his position to help draft the charter's language and push both sides toward agreement. Some historians credit him with supplying the legal framework that gave the document its durability.

cast.name: Pope Innocent III
cast.description: The most powerful pope of the medieval period, Innocent had backed John's restoration to papal favour after a five-year interdict that closed England's churches. When John appealed to him after Runnymede, Innocent annulled the Magna Carta within ten weeks, calling it shameful, demeaning, illegal, and unjust. His annulment made no practical difference — John died the following year, and the charter was reissued under different kings.

cast.name: Robert Fitzwalter
cast.description: The baron who led the armed rebellion against John and styled himself 'Marshal of the Army of God and Holy Church.' Fitzwalter had personal grievances against the king as well as political ones. His coalition held London and forced John to negotiate. Once the charter was annulled and John died, the rebel movement collapsed, but the document it produced endured.

cast.name: The Twenty-Five Barons
cast.description: Clause 61 created a council of twenty-five barons with the legal right to seize royal lands and castles if the king violated the charter. It was the Magna Carta's enforcement mechanism — and the clause that made it a direct threat to royal authority. Pope Innocent cited it specifically when annulling the document. No later reissue included it.

cast.name: Free Men
cast.description: The liberties of the Magna Carta were granted to 'all free men of our kingdom.' In 1215, free men were a legal category — not serfs, not villeins, not the majority of the population. Over subsequent centuries, as serfdom declined and the legal definition of freedom expanded, the charter's protections expanded with it. The phrase became universal only by being repeatedly reinterpreted beyond its original scope.
